sections.text: Structs and enums can have type parameters too. Here is a Point whose coordinates can be any type, as long as x and y are the same type:

Point<T> declares T after the name, then uses it for the fields. Rust works out T from the values: whole is a Point<i32> and fractional is a Point<f64>. A method may share a name with a field: whole.x() calls the method, while whole.y reads the field.

Look at impl<T> Point<T>. The first <T> declares the placeholder, just like in a generic function. Without it Rust would think T is a real type named T. The second one, in Point<T>, says which type the impl is for. Writing the whole thing out once is how you say "for every Point, whatever T is".

Both fields share one T, so mixing types is an error. Point { x: 5, y: 4.0 } does not compile: Rust fixes T as an integer from x, then finds a float in y (error E0308, mismatched types). If you want two different types, use two type parameters, Point<T, U>.
You can also write an impl for one specific type. This method only exists for Point<f64>, because it needs square roots:
You have already used generic types. Option<T> and Result<T, E> are plain enums with type parameters. Their real definitions in the standard library look like this:

So Option<i32> is "an Option holding an i32", and Result<u32, String> is "a Result that is Ok with a u32 or Err with a String". Vec<T> is the same idea: a generic struct, so Vec<i32> and Vec<String> are different types made from one definition. Here is a small generic type of our own that wraps a Vec<T>:

Rust can work out T from the later push calls, so the annotation Stack<String> is not strictly needed here. Writing it makes the code clearer, and you do need it when nothing later says what T is. last() on a Vec returns an Option holding a reference to the final item, or None if the Vec is empty. peek reuses that.

Stack<T> is generic over any T, even types you have not seen yet. That is the whole point: one definition, and the compiler builds the right version for each T you use. If it helps, picture Vec<T> as a box labelled "T goes here".

Like List<T> in Java/C# or std::vector<T> in C++. Unlike Java there is no type erasure and no boxing; like C# and C++, Stack<i32> stores plain i32 values. Option<T> is Rust's replacement for null, and Result<T, E> replaces thrown exceptions. Both are ordinary generic enums, not language magic.

exercise.prompt: Pair only holds i32 values, so the Pair of words in main doesn't compile. Make it generic so it can hold any type, and keep swapped working. It should print two lines: 2 1 and b a. Hint: struct Pair<T>, impl<T> Pair<T>, and fn swapped(self) -> Pair<T>.

tests.label: Swapping 1 and 2 gives 2 and 1
tests.code:
let p = Pair { left: 1, right: 2 }.swapped();
check_eq!((p.left, p.right), (2, 1));

tests.label: Swapping a and b gives b and a
tests.code:
let p = Pair { left: "a", right: "b" }.swapped();
check_eq!((p.left, p.right), ("b", "a"));

tests.label: The program prints 2 1, then b a
owned Strings
tests.code:
let p = Pair { left: String::from("x"), right: String::from("y") }.swapped();
check_eq!((p.left, p.right), (String::from("y"), String::from("x")));

tests.label: floats
tests.code:
let p = Pair { left: 1.5, right: 2.5 }.swapped();
check_eq!((p.left, p.right), (2.5, 1.5));

tests.label: swapping twice gives the original, with chars
tests.code:
let p = Pair { left: 'a', right: 'b' }.swapped().swapped();
check_eq!((p.left, p.right), ('a', 'b'));

tests.label: T has no bounds: any type works

hints: Pair only works with i32 right now. Making it generic touches three places: the struct, the impl line, and the type swapped returns. Look back at how the lesson made Point generic.
Declare T after the struct name, Pair<T>, and use it for both fields. The impl needs T twice: impl<T> Pair<T>. Then swapped returns Pair<T>.
Once Pair<T> is generic, the Pair of words in main works with no other change: swapped hands back a Pair with left and right swapped.

quiz.question: Why is it written impl<T> Point<T> and not just impl Point<T>?
options: The first <T> chooses the one concrete type that every Point will hold from then on
The first <T> declares T as a placeholder, so Rust does not look for a real type named T
The first <T> makes only the return types of the methods generic, not their parameters
quiz.explanation: In impl<T> Point<T>, the first <T> declares T, so Rust knows it is a placeholder and doesn't look for a real type with that name. Without it, Point<T> would mean a type literally called T.

quiz.question: What is Option<T>?
options: A generic struct with a value field and an is_present flag
A keyword the compiler handles specially, with no definition in the library
A generic enum with two variants, Some(T) and None
quiz.explanation: Option<T> is an ordinary generic enum in the standard library, defined as enum Option<T> { None, Some(T) }. It isn't a struct with a flag, and it isn't special syntax of the compiler.

quiz.question: Why does Point { x: 5, y: 4.0 } fail when both fields of Point<T> have type T?
options: x and y share one T, but 5 is an integer and 4.0 is a float
Point can only be created with integer values in its fields
Floats cannot be stored in generic structs, only in ordinary ones
quiz.explanation: Both fields use the same T, so x and y must have the same type. 5 is an integer and 4.0 is a float, so the compiler rejects it. Generic structs hold floats fine, and you can use two parameters, Point<T, U>, to allow different types.
